cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, is writing to Timothy, his beloved child (2 Timothy 1:1-2). He just told Timothy to be kind to everyone and to gently correct the people who oppose him (2 Timothy 2:24-25). Now Paul says, "But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come."

cards.question: Paul tells Timothy that terrible times will come in the last days. What does he say will make them so terrible?

cards.text: So Paul starts a list, and friend, this list does NOT quit: lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy.
He's STILL going: unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, traitorous, reckless, conceited. And I thought MY mustache went on forever.

cards.question: Paul's list started with people who love themselves and love money. Near the end, he says they'll be lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of who?
Paul says the people on this list have a form of godliness.

cards.text: They have a form of godliness, but they deny its power. That's a cookie box with a perfect gold bow on top, and you open it up and it's just... crumbs.

cards.question: These people have a form of godliness but deny its power. What does Paul tell Timothy to do about people like these?

cards.text: Paul says they're the kind who worm their way into households. They captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions.

cards.question: Paul says these women are always learning. What's the catch?

answers.text: They never come to know the truth
They never share what they learn
They forget it all by morning

cards.text: Always learning, never getting there: that's me reading the same cookie recipe every night for a year and STILL asking which one's the oven. Then Paul reaches way back for two names: Jannes and Jambres.

cards.question: Paul compares these men to Jannes and Jambres. Jannes and Jambres opposed ___.
Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, Israel's leader. Paul says these men oppose the ___ in the same way.

cards.text: Paul doesn't tiptoe around it, friend. He says these men are depraved in mind.

cards.question: Paul says these men still stand approved in the faith.
Paul says these men will keep advancing further and further.
Just like with Jannes and Jambres, Paul says these men's folly will be ___ to everyone.

findings.problem: The opening card is three sentences of plain setup and a quote, with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a reference note, not the storyteller opening the passage.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question says "these women" without saying who they are. It points back to card 9, which is no longer on screen. It should say something like the women these men captivate.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't hold together. Reading a cookie recipe over and over has nothing to do with not knowing which appliance is the oven. The comparison doesn't match the core action of always learning but never coming to the truth, and a stranger would say "huh?"

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "Paul says these men still stand approved in the faith" doesn't say who "these men" are. The baker can't see the earlier cards. The question should give the context, such as the men who oppose the truth like Jannes and Jambres.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "Paul says these men will keep advancing further and further" doesn't say who "these men" are. The question needs its own context.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Jannes and Jambres show up for the first time with no description of who they are. Scripture names them only here, and the only thing the text says about them is that they opposed Moses. Saying that on this card would give away the answer to card 12. The usual identification, Pharaoh's magicians (compare Exodus 7:11), comes from tradition, not from the text. In the same way, Moses first appears as an answer on card 12 and isn't introduced until card 13.
findings.question: How should Papa Dorin introduce someone the Bible describes only by the fact a later choice card asks about? Should the new-people rule give way to the never-give-away rule here, with the name left for the dictionary pop-up? Or should he use a neutral description, and if so, can he call Jannes and Jambres Pharaoh's magicians when no verse names them that way?
